subtype: Pacing and fidgeting for energy or worry [Expressing]
passage: Farida paced up and down the corridor outside the science room, back and forth, her hands swinging. The test would start in five minutes. Nandini watched her from the bench. “Are you nervous?” “A bit,” said Farida. “But I'm also bursting with energy. I can't sit still.” Nandini nodded. “Want to walk to the water cooler and back with me?” They walked fast, and Farida stopped swinging her hands. When the bell rang, she sat down at her desk and took a deep breath. Her leg still bounced a little, but she began to write.

qa.q: Where did Farida pace before the test?
qa.a: She paced up and down the corridor outside the science room.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling as she paced, and what else does it show?
qa.a: A mix of nerves and extra energy, since she said she was a bit nervous but also bursting with energy. Moving helped her settle.

qa.q: What small step helped Farida focus before the test?
qa.a: Nandini offered a brisk walk to the water cooler and back, so the energy had somewhere to go before she sat.

qa.q: How might Nandini see Farida's pacing?
qa.a: She wondered if it was nerves, so she asked instead of assuming, and offered help. She may feel glad to be a support.

grounding: Pacing before a test can show nerves, excitement or a need for movement; movement helps focus.

subtype: Pacing and fidgeting for energy or worry [Expressing]
passage:
“Sit still, Santosh,” said Lalit Mama, looking up from his newspaper. “Your leg is shaking the whole table.”
“I am sitting still.”
“Your leg is bouncing. Are you doing it to annoy me?”
“No. It helps me think. My head gets stuck otherwise.”
Lalit Mama put the paper down. “Hmm. Stuck how?”
“Like sums go slow.”
“Then do ten jumps in the yard, come back and try again. And bounce the leg if it helps, but under the table.”
Santosh grinned. “Okay!”

qa.q: What did Lalit Mama say Santosh's leg was doing to the table?
qa.a: He said it was shaking the whole table.

qa.q: Why was Santosh bouncing his leg, and how did Lalit Mama first read it?
qa.a: He said it helps him think because his head gets stuck otherwise. Lalit Mama first wondered if he was doing it to annoy him.

qa.q: What could help Santosh focus on his sums?
qa.a: A short movement break, such as the ten jumps in the yard Lalit Mama suggested, and permission to bounce the leg quietly under the table.

qa.q: How might Lalit Mama feel when he hears Santosh's reason?
qa.a: Probably a bit surprised and glad he asked, and less annoyed once he understood. He then offered a practical fix.

grounding: Leg bouncing can show a need for movement rather than defiance; movement breaks help focus.

subtype: Pacing and fidgeting for energy or worry [Expressing]
passage: I'm Deepak. Last year, my leg never stopped bouncing in tuition. Nilesh Sir would say, “Deepak, still!” and I'd freeze it, and then my whole brain went into keeping the leg still instead of the sums. One evening before the unit test, I was pacing the corridor, round and round, and Sir came out. I thought I was in trouble. Instead he said, “Is it nerves or energy?” I said, “Both, I think.” He said, “Then walk to the gate and back, twice, and come in.” I did, and sat down calmer. After that he gave the whole group a stretch break every twenty minutes. My sums got better.

qa.q: How often did Sir give the group a stretch break?
qa.a: Sir gave the group a stretch break every twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling while pacing before the test?
qa.a: Deepak was nervous and full of energy, and at first worried about being in trouble when Sir came out.

qa.q: Why did the stretch breaks help?
qa.a: They let Deepak use up energy instead of spending effort keeping still, which helped with focus on the sums.

qa.q: How did Nilesh Sir first see the bouncing leg?
qa.a: Nilesh Sir first saw it as something to stop, not realising keeping still took all Deepak's attention.

grounding: Shows a child pacing and bouncing a leg from nerves and energy, and movement breaks helping focus.

subtype: Pacing and fidgeting for energy or worry [Expressing]
passage: Class note, Tuesday. Sunaina, Class 3. Thomas's file from last year says “defiant, won't stay seated.” After two weeks, I don't see defiance. I see a boy who is up and down, jiggling and drumming, especially after long sitting or before tests, but who says sorry and sits again when I ask. So this week I gave him jobs: carrying the register, cleaning the board, handing out copies. After each errand he sits and works for a good stretch. Today, before the spelling test, he paced by the window for a minute, then sat down and got his best score yet. I've told his parents we'll keep the movement breaks.

qa.q: What did Thomas's file from last year say?
qa.a: It said “defiant, won't stay seated.”

qa.q: What might Thomas be feeling when he paces before a test?
qa.a: He is probably nervous or restless with energy, and moving helps him settle rather than being a sign of defiance.

qa.q: Why did Sunaina's errands work?
qa.a: They gave Thomas a regular chance to move, so he could sit and work for a good stretch afterwards.

qa.q: How did last year's teacher read Thomas's movement?
qa.a: Last year's teacher read it as defiance, perhaps without trying movement breaks to see if they helped.

grounding: Shows an energetic child who fidgets and paces being misread as defiant, and movement breaks helping focus.

subtype: Pacing and fidgeting for energy or worry [Expressing]
passage: Saturday. Lakshmi's diary. The recital was at six. From four o'clock I couldn't sit. I walked from my room to the kitchen to the balcony and back, again and again, and when Amma made me sit to eat, my leg bounced so hard the plate rattled. Siddharth said, “Relax, why are you so scared?” But I wasn't scared, not mostly. It felt like fizzy water inside me, like I had to move or I'd pop. Amma said, “Go dance through your piece in the hall once.” I did it twice, and afterwards I could eat. On stage I didn't miss a single step. I'm still fizzy now.

qa.q: What time was the recital?
qa.a: The recital was at six.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling while pacing before the recital?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt mostly excited, fizzy inside with energy, rather than scared as Siddharth thought.

qa.q: Why was Amma's idea helpful?
qa.a: Dancing through the piece used up the energy, so Lakshmi could eat and feel ready.

qa.q: How did Siddharth read the pacing?
qa.a: Siddharth read it as fear, missing that it was mostly excitement and a need to move.

grounding: Shows a child pacing and bouncing a leg from excitement rather than fear, and movement helping them settle.

subtype: Pacing and fidgeting for energy or worry [Expressing]
passage:
The bus to the block science fair was late, and the kasba bus stand smelled of diesel and roasted peanuts. Swati couldn't sit. She paced from the tea stall to the timetable board and back, then sat and bounced her knee so hard the bench shook.

"Arre, beta, sit still!" said an old man beside her.

Mehak, holding their model of a water filter, watched her. "Scared or excited?"
"Both. And my legs just need to go."

Mehak stood up. "Then let's walk and practise our lines." Up and down they went, past the peanut cart, saying the steps aloud. By the tenth lap, Swati knew every word. Then the bus honked round the corner.

qa.q: What model was Mehak holding?
qa.a: Their model of a water filter.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling as she paced and bounced her knee?
qa.a: A mix of nervous and excited about the science fair, as she says herself, with energy that needed to move.

qa.q: Which choice helped Swati focus?
qa.a: Mehak turned the fidgeting into a walk while they practised their lines, so the movement helped Swati learn every word.

qa.q: How did the old man on the bench see Swati's bouncing?
qa.a: He saw it as restless fidgeting that should stop, not knowing it was her way of handling nerves and excitement.

grounding: It shows a child pacing and bouncing a leg before an event from nerves, excitement and energy, and a movement break helping her focus.
